sourceEnglish.objective: greet staff, learn whether to order at the counter, and find a place
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Walk into a crowded Roman café and work out how ordering and seating operate.
englishWordAnchors: Good morning, do I order here at the counter?
Do I sit wherever I want?
Sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat, please?
Is it to go or to eat here?
englishReading: A traveler enters a very busy café.
There is a long line in front of the counter.
The traveler says: Good morning.
He asks the waitress: Do I order here at the counter?
The waitress answers: Yes, order here, please.
He asks: Is there a free table?
The waitress says: There is a table on the patio.
He waits in line and looks at the menu.
Then he orders a coffee and a sweet pastry.

lessons.title: Entering a busy café
lessons.objective: Greet staff, ask whether to order at the counter, and find out if a seat is available.
lessons.focus: In a Japanese café, counter and seating practices vary. 注文はここでいいですか asks where to order. 空いていますか asks whether a seat is free. Check with staff rather than sitting or assuming a universal rule.
lessons.scene: Sam enters a busy café near a station and asks the staff how to order.

sourceEnglish.roleplay: Order a local coffee without assuming the names or customs are the same as at home.

I want a coffee with milk, please.
Is it to drink here or to go?

lessons.title: Choosing a coffee
lessons.objective: Ask what coffee is offered, check milk and size options, then state whether you will drink it there.
lessons.focus: ブレンド and アメリカン are menu labels, not universal translations of black coffee. Ask what a shop offers. 牛乳 and オーツミルク are ingredients, but availability and allergy safety require confirmation. ～にできますか asks whether a change is possible.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask what is fresh, filled, sweet, savory, or typical
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Ask the server to explain three pastries and recommend one made that morning.
englishWordAnchors: Which one is the most typical?
Which one came out of the oven today?

lessons.title: Choosing a pastry
lessons.objective: Ask what was baked this morning, whether an item is filled, and which pastry the staff recommends.

sourceEnglish.objective: request eggs, sides, toast, fruit, and cooking preferences
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Build a complete hot breakfast order and confirm what is included.
englishWordAnchors: I want two scrambled eggs, please.
englishReading: A traveler walks into a café in the morning.
He sits at a table and looks at the menu.
The waitress asks: What would you like?
He says: I want two scrambled eggs, please.
He also orders bacon, toast, and fruit.
The waitress asks: How do you want the eggs?
He answers: I want them well done, without salt.
Then he asks: Is the coffee included?
The waitress says: Yes, the coffee is included.

lessons.title: Ordering a full breakfast
lessons.objective: Order eggs and sides, state a cooking preference, and ask which items are included.
lessons.focus: ～をお願いします makes a polite order. 焼き加減 means cooking level; よく焼いてください requests well cooked. セットに含まれますか checks whether something is included. Menu contents and cooking choices vary; do not imply a fixed breakfast set.
lessons.scene: Sam sees an egg breakfast set on a café menu and asks what comes with it.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask whether breakfast is included, the hours, room number, and buffet rules
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Arrive at a hotel breakfast and resolve uncertainty about access and seating.
englishWordAnchors: Can I sit at any table?
Excuse me, what are the buffet rules?
englishReading: A traveler arrives at the hotel dining room in the morning.
He talks to the receptionist: Is breakfast included?
She says: Yes, it is included with your room.
He asks: What are the breakfast hours?
She answers that the hours are from 6:30 to 10:00, according to the hotel.
The traveler gives his room number: 214.
Then he asks: Is it a buffet or a menu?
She explains the buffet rules: take a clean plate and do not take food with you.
He looks for a free table and gets coffee.

lessons.title: Checking hotel breakfast
lessons.objective: Ask whether your room plan includes breakfast, confirm the hours, and ask how the buffet works.
lessons.focus: 朝食付き means breakfast included in a particular booking; it is not assumed. 何時から何時まで asks the hours. 部屋番号 is room number. Follow the hotel’s stated buffet rules rather than treating one hotel’s practice as universal.
lessons.scene: At the hotel dining-room entrance, Sam gives a room number and checks the booking.

sourceEnglish.objective: state an allergy or dietary need and confirm ingredients without seeking medical advice
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Ask whether a breakfast item contains nuts, dairy, gluten, meat, or another ingredient.
englishWordAnchors: I have an allergy to nuts.
Can you check with the kitchen, please?
englishReading: I am in a café and I talk to the server before ordering.
First I say: I have an allergy to nuts.
Then I ask: What ingredients does it have?
The server is not sure, so he is going to check with the kitchen.
Afterward he tells me that, according to the kitchen, the bread has no nuts.
I also say: I don't eat meat, and I ask if the filling has meat in it.
If the kitchen is not sure, I order something else.
I only confirm the ingredients and I do not ask for medical advice.

lessons.title: State a food restriction
lessons.objective: Tell staff about a nut allergy or food preference, ask the kitchen to check ingredients and handling, and decline when the answer is uncertain.
lessons.focus: アレルギーがあります states an allergy; 肉を食べません states a preference and must not be conflated. 原材料 asks about ingredients; 調理器具 asks about utensils and possible shared handling. A statement that an ingredient is absent does not prove a dish is safe. If staff cannot confirm, do not order that dish. This language is a communication draft pending qualified food-allergy review, not medical advice.
lessons.scene: Sam asks about a pastry for a companion with a nut allergy; staff cannot verify its preparation.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask for a typical regional breakfast and understand a cultural explanation
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Tell the server you want the breakfast locals actually choose, not a tourist substitute.
englishWordAnchors: What do people here eat for breakfast?
I want the breakfast that locals order.
I don't want something just for tourists.
Can you recommend a typical dish to me?
Can you explain to me what it has in it?
Can you repeat that more slowly, please?
englishReading: Ana sits at a table in a small café in Puebla.
First she asks the server: What do people here eat for breakfast?
Then she says: I want the breakfast that locals order.
The server smiles and says that chilaquiles are a typical morning dish.
According to him, they are going to serve the chilaquiles with green salsa and beans.
Ana asks: Can you explain to me what it has in it?
The server explains that café de olla comes with cinnamon and that the sweet bread is for afterward.
Ana orders the chilaquiles, a café de olla, and a sweet bread.
At the end, she is going to pay at the counter.

lessons.title: Ask about a local breakfast
lessons.objective: Ask staff what people in the area choose for breakfast, hear the explanation, and check the ingredients before ordering.
lessons.focus: この辺りでは means around here; この店では means at this shop. 「地元の人は」 asks about local customers without claiming everyone eats the same thing. A recommendation is one staff member’s description, not a universal cultural fact or ingredient guarantee.

The waiter smiles and says: Everything is right, I'll bring it right away.
At the end, I ask for the check at the table.

lessons.title: Order for a group
lessons.objective: Order different drinks and foods for three people, then read back who receives each item.
lessons.focus: ～には marks the person receiving an item. それぞれ means each person. こちらは誰の分ですか asks whose portion an item is. Japanese often uses a person’s name rather than a bare pronoun. Avoid mixing an allergy need with an ordinary taste preference.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask for food or coffee to go, packaging, napkins, and utensils
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Convert part of a seated order into takeaway because your train leaves soon.
englishWordAnchors: Can I order the coffee to go?
I want this to go, please.
Can you give me napkins and a spoon?
Can you put it in a bag for me?
Does it come with a lid?
englishReading: A traveler is in a café and looks at the clock.
First he orders a coffee with milk and a croissant at the counter.
Then he says: Excuse me, can I order the coffee to go?
The waitress asks: Do you want a lid and a bag?
The traveler answers: Yes, please, and I also need napkins and a spoon.
After that he changes the croissant order, because he is going to eat on the train.
He says: Can you put it in a paper bag for me?
In the end he pays the bill and says thank you.
With his order in hand, he quickly heads out to the station.

lessons.title: Change part of an order to takeaway
lessons.objective: Ask to take a coffee and pastry away, check packaging, and request a napkin or spoon.

lessons.scene: Sam has limited time before a train and asks the café to change the unprepared part of an order.

The waitress brings the card terminal, he pays, and he asks her for the receipt.
Before leaving, the traveler checks the total and says thank you.

lessons.title: Understand the bill
lessons.objective: Ask for the bill, clarify an unfamiliar item, confirm the total and payment method, then request a receipt.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask how food is handled, whether tongs, toasters, or milk jugs are shared, and decide what to order
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Your friend has a serious nut allergy; ask how pastries are stored and handled before ordering anything for them.
englishWordAnchors: My friend is allergic to nuts.
How do you store the pastries?
Do you use the same tongs for everything?
Do you share the toaster and the milk jug?
Can you show me the ingredients, please?
I'm going to order a black coffee, no pastry.
englishReading: This morning, Elena and I arrived at the counter of a small café.
First, I told the barista: My friend is allergic to nuts.
Then I asked: How do you store the pastries in the display case?
The barista explained: The bread with nuts is in the same display case, and sometimes we use the same tongs.
I also asked: Do you share the toaster and the milk jug?
He answered: Yes, and we use the same jug for the almond milk.
Then he said: There is a risk of cross-contact at this counter.
So Elena decided: I'm going to order a black coffee, no pastry.

lessons.title: Ask about shared handling
lessons.objective: Explain a companion’s nut allergy, ask about shared utensils and preparation, and decline an item when handling cannot be verified.
lessons.focus: 共用 means shared. 同じトングを使いますか asks whether the same tongs are used; 調理器具 asks about kitchen tools. An ingredient label is insufficient to establish allergy safety, and even a plain drink must not be assumed safe. This is communication practice pending qualified food-allergy review, not medical advice.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask why standing and sitting prices differ and choose where to drink your coffee
sourceEnglish.roleplay: You notice the table price is higher than the counter price; ask how pricing works and decide where to sit.
englishWordAnchors: Why is it more expensive at the table?
How much does it cost on the terrace?
I am going to have my coffee at the counter.
Is there a surcharge for the terrace?
I prefer to sit at a table, please.
englishReading: I go into a small café and look at the menu on the wall.
The menu says: coffee with milk, 2 euros at the counter and 3 euros at the table.
First I ask the waiter: Why is it more expensive at the table?
He explains: At the table there is table service, and on the terrace there is a surcharge.
Then I ask: How much does it cost on the terrace?
The waiter answers: According to the menu, it costs 4 euros.
I am in a hurry, so I say: I am going to have my coffee at the counter.
After that I pay the bill at the counter and leave a small tip.

lessons.title: Compare two posted prices
lessons.objective: Ask why one café posts different prices for counter and table service, then choose where to drink coffee.
lessons.focus: カウンター席 and テーブル席 name seating areas. 店内利用 means eating or drinking in the shop. 料金が違うのはなぜですか asks why prices differ. This is a fictional menu example; a counter/table surcharge is not a general Japanese café rule. Confirm the posted total before ordering.
lessons.scene: A café menu displays one price at the counter and another at a table; Sam asks staff what applies.

sourceEnglish.objective: show what your booking promised, question the charge calmly, and agree on a corrected bill
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Your hotel bills you for breakfast your booking says is included; resolve it calmly with the front desk.
englishWordAnchors: I think there is a mistake on the bill.
My booking says breakfast is included.
Can you explain this charge to me?
Can you remove the charge, please?
Can you give me a new receipt, please?
englishReading: Before leaving the hotel, I check the bill at the front desk.
I see a charge of 36 dollars for breakfast.
I calmly tell the receptionist: I think there is a mistake on the bill.
First I show him the confirmation email on my phone and say: My booking says breakfast is included.
He checks my room rate on the computer.
Then he says: You are right, I am going to remove the charge.
I ask him: Can you give me a new receipt, please?
In the end, I pay the corrected bill without the breakfast.

lessons.title: Question a hotel breakfast charge
lessons.objective: Show a booking confirmation, ask about a breakfast charge, and request a corrected bill only after the desk verifies the plan.
lessons.focus: 予約確認メール is booking confirmation email. 朝食付き means breakfast included in a specific booking. 明細 is the itemized bill. ～ようですが expresses tentative observation without declaring staff wrong. Ask the desk to check the booked rate before asking for correction.

sourceEnglish.objective: state a seating preference, explain your reason, and accept or propose a compromise
sourceEnglish.roleplay: A server asks your group to move to a smaller table for a reservation; explain why you'd like to stay and reach a compromise.
englishWordAnchors: We prefer this table because we have a stroller.
What time does the reservation arrive?
If possible, we would like to stay here.
englishReading: It is Saturday morning and my family is having breakfast at a big table by the window.
The server comes over and says: Excuse me, we have a reservation and we need this table.
She offers us a smaller table in the corner, near the counter.
I calmly explain to her: We prefer this table because we have a stroller and it does not fit in the corner.
Then I ask her: What time does the reservation arrive?
The server answers that the group arrives at 10:30.
So I propose: What if we finish breakfast here before 10:15 and then move to the patio for coffee?
She smiles and says: Perfect, there is shade on the patio and I will bring you an extra chair.
I tell her: Thank you very much for your help, this way we are all happy.

lessons.title: Negotiate a table change
lessons.objective: Explain why a smaller table will not fit a stroller, ask when a reservation begins, and agree on a workable alternative.
lessons.focus: ベビーカーが入らない means a stroller will not fit. 予約は何時からですか asks the reserved time. ～なら expresses a conditional compromise. Do not block exits or aisles; the staff and group should inspect the offered space before agreeing.
lessons.scene: Staff needs a reserved table; Sam’s family checks another space that can fit the stroller.

sourceEnglish.objective: learn local habits about milky coffee, sugar, lingering, and paying first
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Ask a barista which café habits mark someone as a tourist and how long it is fine to stay at a table.
englishWordAnchors: Do you pay first at the register here?
Does the coffee already come with sugar?
Is it okay to stay at the table for a while?
What habits are typical of tourists here?
Can I order another cortado later?
englishReading: A traveler walks into a small café and asks the barista: Do you pay first at the register here?
The barista smiles and explains: In this café, yes, you pay first at the register and then order at the counter.
She orders a cortado because in the morning she prefers less milk than in a café con leche.
Then she asks: Does the coffee already come with sugar?
He answers: No, the sugar is on the counter, so you add as much as you want.
The traveler also wants to know: What habits are typical of tourists here?
The barista says: Many tourists wait for the bill at the table, but here there is no bill at the end, and if there are free tables, nobody asks them to leave.
Before sitting down, she asks: Is it okay to stay at the table for a while? Can I order another cortado later?
The barista answers: Of course, take your time; if you want another cortado, you pay for it at the register, and the tip is optional.

lessons.title: Ask how this café works
lessons.objective: Ask where to pay, whether sugar is included, and whether another order is needed to stay longer.
lessons.focus: この店では (at this shop) limits a question to the current café. 先にお会計ですか asks whether payment comes first. ～てもいいですか asks permission; do not generalize one café’s policy to a region.
lessons.scene: A traveler asks staff about this café’s payment and seating rules before ordering.

sourceEnglish.objective: ask a local for a specific recommendation, opening hours, and walking directions
sourceEnglish.roleplay: Ask the hotel host where to find the best bakery open before 7 a.m. and how to walk there.
englishWordAnchors: Can you recommend a bakery nearby?
How do I get there on foot from here?
englishReading: It is 6:30 in the morning and Ana is looking for breakfast near the hotel.
Ana asks the receptionist: Can you recommend a bakery nearby that is open before 7?
The receptionist says: I recommend Panadería Lupita, because the sweet bread comes out hot very early.
Ana asks: What time does it open?
He answers: According to their hours, it opens at 6, but on Sundays it opens later.
Then Ana asks: How do I get there on foot from here?
The receptionist shows her the map and says: Walk 3 blocks along this street and turn right at the traffic light.
Ana does not understand everything and asks: Can you repeat that, please?
He calmly repeats: The bakery is on the corner, across from the square.

lessons.title: Find a bakery open early
lessons.objective: Ask hotel staff for a nearby bakery, verify its current opening time, and repeat walking directions.
lessons.focus: 近くのパン屋 (nearby bakery), 何時に開きますか (what time does it open?) and もう一度お願いします (please repeat) form a practical route request. Hours and routes can change, so confirm with current local information.

sourceEnglish.objective: alert staff, ask someone to call emergency services, give the location, and describe what you saw
sourceEnglish.roleplay: A guest at the next table collapses; alert the staff, ask for emergency help, and describe what happened.
englishWordAnchors: Can you call an ambulance, please?
A man fell at the next table.
What is the exact address of the café?
I don't know if he is breathing well.
We are on the corner of Juárez and Madero.
englishReading: I am having breakfast in a café when the customer at the next table falls to the floor.
I stand up and say to the waiter: Help, please, it's an emergency!
The manager comes quickly and I ask him: Can you call an ambulance, please?
He dials the emergency number and the operator asks him for the address.
The manager answers: We are on the corner of Juárez and Madero, next to the bank.
Then the operator wants to know what happened, because that information helps the paramedics.
I explain to her: A man fell at the next table and he isn't answering.
I also tell her: I don't know if he is breathing well.
Then I wait at the door to show the table to the paramedics when they arrive.

lessons.title: Call for help at a café
lessons.objective: Alert staff to a collapse, ask them to call local emergency services, and report only the location and what you observed.
lessons.focus: 助けてください (please help) and 救急車を呼んでください (please call an ambulance) are urgent requests. Report 見たこと (what you saw) without diagnosis. Confirm the exact location and use the local emergency service number; medical and regional procedures require qualified review.
lessons.scene: A guest sees another customer collapse and immediately alerts café staff.

Ana takes a breath and says: Could you bring me cold water, please?
The server brings a glass of cold water and some napkins, and Ana carefully dries her arm.

The manager brings the first-aid kit and says: If the burn hurts a lot, we can call a doctor.

englishReading: It is Tuesday morning and Lena walks into a small café with her laptop.
Before sitting down, she goes to the counter and asks the server: Do you mind if I stay and work for 2 hours?
The server smiles and says: No problem, but at lunchtime it gets very full.
Lena answers: If it fills up, I'll give up the table, and then she asks: What is the Wi-Fi password?
The server gives her a slip of paper with the password and points her to a table in the corner with an outlet.
Lena plugs in her charger, orders a latte and a sweet pastry, and starts working.
After 1 hour, she raises her hand and asks: When would you prefer that I order again?
The server says: Whenever you like, because I come by your table every half hour.
At the end, Lena asks for the bill and leaves a good tip for the time and the space.
